title: Array-as-stack
description: A plain array becomes a stack with push + pop on the same end — LIFO, both O(1).

conversation.intro: How an interview about stack-as-array would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before reaching for a stack — pin down what you're modeling.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I need a data structure where the most-recently-added item comes out first — LIFO. That's a stack. Quick checks before I code:"

• What's the access pattern: pure push/pop, or do I also need to peek?
• Roughly how many items? (Stack-as-array is fine up to ~10^7; truly huge needs a linked list to avoid array growth costs.)
• Do I need any other operations — `size`, `clear`, `contains`? They affect whether I wrap it in a class.
• What's the element type — primitives, or objects I might compare?
sections.why: Naming LIFO explicitly is the magic word — it tells the interviewer you've recognized the abstract pattern, not just chosen a structure by reflex. The 'do I need peek' question is what unlocks the right idiom (`stack.at(-1)`); without it, candidates sometimes pop-then-push to peek and look silly.

sections.title: 2. Why this template?
sections.prompt: Why an array instead of a custom Stack class?
sections.say:
"In JS, a plain array IS a stack — `push` appends to the end, `pop` removes from the end, both O(1) amortized. No need for a wrapper class or a linked list. Three idioms to know:"

• `stack.push(x)` — add to top.
• `stack.pop()` — remove and return the top (or `undefined` if empty).
• `stack.at(-1)` — peek at the top without removing. (Same as `stack[stack.length - 1]` but cleaner.)

"And `while (stack.length)` is the canonical drain loop — `stack.length` is truthy when non-empty."
sections.why: The 'array IS a stack' observation is the boilerplate that lets you skip ceremony. Most interviewers expect this; some still ask candidates to implement a Stack class for warm-up. Knowing both — and reaching for the array idiom unless asked otherwise — signals JS fluency. The `stack.at(-1)` mention beats the older `stack[stack.length - 1]` form.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — when stacks fire
sections.prompt: What problem signals say 'reach for a stack'?
sections.say:
"Three classic stack signals:"

• 'Most recent' / 'last X' — undo history, browser back button, evaluation contexts.
• 'Matching pairs' — balanced brackets, HTML tag matching. Push opens, pop on close, compare the pair.
• 'Backtracking' / DFS — push frame on recursion enter, pop on return. The call stack is itself a stack; explicit-stack DFS just makes it visible.

"For the L3, the pattern is 'reverse order' — and that's the same shape: push everything in, pop everything out, and the order naturally inverts because the last in comes out first."
sections.why: Naming WHY each signal points to a stack — 'most recent' = LIFO matches the data lifecycle, 'matching pairs' = nesting is inherently last-opened-first-closed — distinguishes derivation from pattern-matching. Reverse-as-LIFO is the connection that takes the abstract pattern and shows you see why it solves THIS problem.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: Three cases — the L3 prompt input, a single-character string, and an empty string. The interesting ones are the edges that prove the drain loop terminates correctly.

examples.trace:
Push phase:
  'h' → stack=['h']
  'e' → stack=['h','e']
  'l' → stack=['h','e','l']
  'l' → stack=['h','e','l','l']
  'o' → stack=['h','e','l','l','o']
Drain phase (stack.length truthy → pop):
  pop 'o' → out='o', stack=['h','e','l','l']
  pop 'l' → out='ol', stack=['h','e','l']
  pop 'l' → out='oll', stack=['h','e']
  pop 'e' → out='olle', stack=['h']
  pop 'h' → out='olleh', stack=[]
stack empty → return 'olleh' ✓

examples.note: Single char — push once, pop once, identity.
examples.trace:
Push: 'a' → stack=['a']
Drain: pop 'a' → out='a', stack=[]
return 'a' ✓

examples.note: Empty string — the for-loop and the while-loop both no-op. Confirms termination on empty.
examples.trace:
for-loop over '' → no iterations, stack=[]
while(stack.length=0) → never enters
return '' (the initial empty out) ✓

sections.why: The empty-string trace is the edge that proves you read the loop conditions. A careless implementation might use `do…while` (entering at least once) or check `stack.length > 0` outside the condition — both still work, but pointing out that `while (stack.length)` naturally handles empty is the senior touch.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs or coding choices would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges and pitfalls worth flagging:"

• Empty input → for-loop no-op, drain no-op, returns the initial value (empty string here). No special case needed.
• Forgetting that `pop()` returns `undefined` on empty stack → if you don't check `stack.length`, you'd concatenate `'undefined'` strings. The `while (stack.length)` gate prevents this.
• Using `shift()` to drain instead of `pop()` → you'd get FIFO output (same order, not reversed) AND it's O(n) per shift, so the whole thing is O(n²).
• Pushing the whole string then doing `stack.reverse().join('')` — works but defeats the point of demonstrating the stack pattern.
• For non-ASCII strings (e.g. emoji, combined chars) → iterating `for…of` is correct (Unicode-aware); indexing `s[i]` can split a surrogate pair.
sections.why: The `shift()` substitution is the subtle bug — same output for symmetric inputs, but wrong for asymmetric AND quadratic. Calling it out unprompted shows you understand the dual purpose of `pop` (correctness + complexity). The Unicode point is the senior-tier touch that the interviewer may or may not care about.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — one pass to push (n operations), one pass to pop (n operations). Each `push` and `pop` is O(1) amortized — V8's array implementation grows in geometric chunks, so the average cost per push stays constant.

Space is O(n) — the stack holds every character before the drain begins. (`out` also grows to n chars but they share the same n bound.)

The template generalizes: any 'reverse + process' problem is the stack template. Valid-parentheses is the next step up — push opens, pop-and-compare on close. Beyond that, monotonic stacks (next-greater-element, largest-rectangle-in-histogram) reuse the same push/pop/peek primitives with a smarter invariant."
sections.why: The amortized-O(1) defense is the load-bearing claim — interviewers occasionally probe with 'but doesn't array push sometimes re-allocate?' Naming geometric growth shows you understand why amortized analysis applies. Linking to valid-parens and monotonic stacks proves you see this as a template, not a one-off trick.

walkthrough.intro: Step through `reverseString` using an array-as-stack. The push phase loads the stack; the pop phase drains it and builds the result. Use ◀ Prev / ▶ Next, or pick a different example.
trace: yield { line: 2, label: `enter — s='${s}'`, state: { s, stack: [], out: '' } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'init stack = []', state: { s, stack: [...stack], out: '' } };
yield { line: 4, label: `push '${ch}' → stack=${JSON.stringify(stack)}`, state: { s, stack: [...stack], out: '' } };
yield { line: 7, label: `push phase done — stack=${JSON.stringify(stack)}, begin drain`, state: { s, stack: [...stack], out } };
yield { line: 8, label: `pop '${popped}' → out='${out}', stack=${JSON.stringify(stack)}`, state: { s, stack: [...stack], out } };
yield { line: 9, label: `stack empty — return '${out}'`, state: { s, stack: [...stack], out, returns: out } };

notes: Both push and pop are O(1) amortized — the fastest array pattern.
Use stack.length as the truthy "non-empty" check; stack.at(-1) to peek.
When the problem says "most recent", "matching pairs", or "undo", reach for a stack.

questions.q: Which pair of methods turns an array into a stack?

options: Priority order — the lowest-priority item pops first, like Dijkstra's frontier
Insertion order with deduplication — repeated pushes of the same value are merged

questions.q: Time complexity of stack.push and stack.pop?
options: push is O(1), pop is O(n)

questions.q: Which problem is the most natural fit for a stack?
options: Finding the kth smallest element in a stream
Detecting whether a linked list has a cycle

exercises.prompt: Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, then pop twice and log both results.
Use a stack to check whether brackets are balanced.

blanks.hint: strict equality on the open-bracket test
opening bracket goes on the stack
closing bracket must match the top

L3.prompt: Write `reverseString(s)` using a stack: push every char, then pop them back into a result string. Log `reverseString("hello")`.
hints: Push every char onto an array.
Drain with pop while stack.length is truthy.
